part_title: Generalization — Underfitting, Overfitting and Bias–Variance Trade-offs
review_basis: Original numbered AIF Module 03 WebP slides 41–45 visually inspected in sequence; image titles, examples, numbers and diagrams take priority over legacy lesson map.

scenes.title: Model fit: underfitting, good fit and overfitting
scenes.narration: The goal of machine learning is not simply to remember the examples used in training, but to work reliably on new, unseen cases. This slide has three plots. Each horizontal axis is an input feature and each vertical axis is a target value. The blue dots are observed training examples; the yellow curve is a learned prediction. On the left, underfitting is shown by a nearly straight line that misses the curved pattern in the dots. The model is too simple, showing high bias, and performs poorly even on training examples. Bias here means systematic error from the assumptions of the model, not social bias, although fairness is another important topic. In the center, a smooth curve follows the main trend without chasing every dot, giving a reasonable chance of generalizing. The right plot shows overfitting. A wiggly yellow line tries to follow many individual fluctuations, including noise. It may look impressive on training data yet fail on new samples. Below each graph, the landscape imagery gives an intuition about simple, suitably flexible and overly complicated models. Along the very bottom, the complexity arrow increases from left to right. We usually choose model complexity using validation results and test generalization, not by how closely a training curve touches every dot. The takeaway is to find an appropriate balance. Imagine predicting student exam performance: a single crude rule might miss important patterns, while an elaborate rule remembering individual students might fail on the next class. Check: which model is best merely because it has the lowest training error? We cannot know. We need reliable performance on independent unseen data.

scenes.title: Bias: identifying underfitting
scenes.narration: This slide concentrates on high bias, which occurs when a model's assumptions are too restrictive to capture the relationship in the data. Begin on the left. The turquoise data points form a rise-and-fall curve, but the yellow prediction is an almost straight, upward-sloping line. The horizontal axis is the input feature and the vertical axis is the target value. The simple line misses the main nonlinear trend. In the middle, the three-dimensional blue points and flat orange plane repeat the same idea: a linear model cannot capture a more complicated curved relationship. Linear means straight-line or flat-plane behavior in this simplified illustration, while nonlinear allows different shapes. On the right, read the consequences: the model fails to match the training examples, misses important patterns and may perform badly on both familiar and unseen data. The suggested remedies are to use a model with more appropriate flexibility and to add genuinely relevant features if important information is missing. But a more complicated model is not automatically better; it can create overfitting if not evaluated carefully. Think about estimating electricity demand. A model using only the hour of day may miss changes caused by temperature or holidays. Adding relevant inputs could help more than memorizing every previous day. A decision check: if training error and validation error are both consistently high, does that suggest high bias or high variance? High bias or underfitting is a strong possibility, though data quality and other problems should also be checked.

scenes.title: Variance: identifying overfitting
scenes.narration: Now look at high variance. This means that predictions can change considerably when a model is trained on different samples from the same underlying population. High variance is often associated with overfitting, where a model learns random details specific to its training data. Compare the three graphs from left to right. The first straight-line model underfits, missing a curved pattern. The middle smooth curve captures the essential shape and can generalize better. The right yellow line zigzags dramatically between blue sample points. That line can have very low training error but may respond wildly to small differences in the examples it sees. The lower-left photograph of a house connects this to a property-pricing example. Suppose a predictor memorizes unusual details from a small set of houses in one neighborhood. It might predict those houses well but give unreliable values for new homes. The lower-right panel offers two practical directions: simplify or select features carefully to reduce noise, and evaluate across multiple appropriate training and validation splits to test consistency. Techniques like regularization can also discourage unnecessary complexity. Multiple splits can help measure stability, while the final untouched test set is still important for unbiased evaluation. The warning to remember is that outstanding training scores are not sufficient evidence. A model should be judged by results on representative unseen data. If a house-price model is near-perfect on its training list but much worse on validation homes, which issue should we investigate? Overfitting and high variance.

scenes.title: Bias and variance: comparison scenarios
scenes.narration: This visual replaces plots with three archery targets. On the left, three arrows cluster away from the bullseye. That illustrates high bias: predictions are consistently off target. In the center, arrows are spread widely around the target, representing high variance, which means predictions are unstable. On the right, arrows group close to the middle, showing a favorable balance of lower bias and lower variance. These targets are metaphors, not measured statistical estimates; real model diagnostics use training and validation results, error analysis and repeat experiments. Read the text beneath the three pictures. A model with high bias may be too simple and miss important patterns in both training and new data. High variance may arise when a complex model fits noise and performs much better on training examples than new data. A better fit learns a useful relationship without chasing random fluctuations. At the bottom, the decision cue suggests increasing appropriate flexibility when underfitting is the problem, or reducing excessive complexity and adding regularization when overfitting is the problem. A simple analogy is preparing for an exam. Studying only a single oversimplified rule misses many real questions, while memorizing exact answers without understanding can fail when questions change. A strong learner understands transferable concepts. Ask: if the model keeps making a similar systematic mistake on both training and validation examples, which target does that resemble? The left, high-bias target. If results swing widely depending on the training sample, think about high variance.

scenes.title: The bias–variance trade-off
scenes.narration: This final diagram summarizes how model complexity affects generalization. Read the three sections from left to right. The left says too simple, underfitting. Its yellow line barely follows the blue dots, and the flat three-dimensional surface ignores richer variation. This is the high-bias case, where an overly restrictive model misses real structure. The center is labeled just right. The smoother curve captures the broad pattern without matching every tiny fluctuation. The middle surface is more flexible yet not unnecessarily jagged. The right says too complex, overfitting. Its many twists follow incidental training variations, and the complicated surface may fail to predict new samples. Notice that lower bias and lower variance cannot always be achieved simultaneously; selecting complexity is a trade-off and depends on data quantity, noise, features and regularization. The bottom left applies this to house prices: a straight line might overlook important influences, while an extremely wiggly curve may simply memorize individual sales. The bottom-right decision cue recommends the simplest model that performs well on appropriate unseen validation data. We should compare candidate models with a consistent evaluation procedure and reserve the final test set for a fairer result. Do not rely on visual smoothness alone; some real relationships are legitimately complicated. Comprehension check: if a model's training accuracy keeps improving while validation performance gets worse, should we keep adding complexity? Usually no. We should investigate overfitting, consider regularization or simpler alternatives, and select what generalizes to new examples.
